points.en: 1 Timothy 3:4-5: a man who cannot rule his own house well has not shown he can care for God's church, so the home tests his fitness.
The household is the smaller trust by which God tests a man for the larger trust, since the church is the household of God writ large.
The home is the first proving ground of ministry, not the private backdrop to it.
The order is his walk with God first, then his family, then the church.
The church must never be allowed to consume the family, which comes before it.
What he is at home, such as how he treats his wife, shows what he really believes about grace better than his sermons.
Headship is not domination or tyranny, as the world imagines, but leading as Christ led, by laying himself down in service.
Ephesians 5:25 requires husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
A husband's authority is real, but it is the authority of one who washes feet.
Fathers must not provoke their children to wrath by harshness, inconsistency or double standards.
Fathers must bring children up in the training and admonition of the Lord, instructing and pointing them to Him.
Warning: many pastors' children are driven from Christ not by the gospel preached but by the bitterness bred at home.
Marriage is a covenant joined by God, not a contract dissolved at will; the biblical default is permanence.
The New Testament names grounds like sexual immorality and desertion by an unbelieving spouse, and faithful believers differ on how far the exceptions extend, including remarriage.
The pastor must avoid two errors: cheapening the covenant by treating divorce as easy, and crushing the divorced as beyond grace.
Singleness is no second-class calling; Jesus was single and Paul commended it as a gift.
Sexual purity is required of every servant of God, married and single alike.
The married man guards purity by cherishing his wife and the single man by chastity, both fleeing temptation as Joseph did.
First pressure: the fishbowl, where his wife and children live under congregational scrutiny and unrealistic expectations, and he should shield them.
Second, graver pressure: the endless work of ministry slowly steals the pastor from his family, so the church becomes a mistress of his heart and hours.
Remedy: guard his days, protect family time, and say no to good things to keep the best.
Gaining the whole church while losing his own children profits nothing; a thriving ministry on a neglected family is a tragedy though it looks respectable.
To prevent it he must guard his time and say no to good things in order to protect the best things, putting his family first.
The pastor keeps the faith first of all in his own household, the small flock that bears his name.
Tending his family well makes him a better shepherd of the larger flock, and neglecting it cannot be made up by public success.
The family is a test of fitness because how he handles the smaller household shows whether he can be trusted with the church.
It is a witness because his real beliefs about grace, patience and love show most truly in how he lives at home, more than in his sermons.
